title: The interplay between additive and symmetric large sets and their combinatorial applications

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The second equality for the elementary symmetric polynomial is written as a sum over all nonempty subsets G, but it omits the condition |G|=j. As written, the right-hand side sums over subsets of all sizes, not just size j.

It is claimed that (Z,⊙_{l,k}) is an abelian group when l divides k(k-1). This is false. For example, with l=1,k=1, a⊙b=ab+a+b has identity 0 but most elements have no inverse: a=1 requires (a+1)(b+1)=1, i.e. 2(b+1)=1, with no integer solution b.

The characterizations of thick and syndetic sets state 'there exists a left ideal L such that L⊆A' and 'for every left ideal L, L∩A≠∅'. But L is a subset of βS, while A is a subset of S. These should involve the closure A-bar: L⊆\overline{A} and L∩\overline{A}≠∅.

The theorem asserts cl(K(βZ,+))∩K((βZ,⊙_t))≠∅. But in (Z,⊙_t) the integer t is a zero element, so K(βZ,⊙_t) is the principal ultrafilter {t}; this is disjoint from cl(K(βZ,+)). The proof also chooses n∈Z* rather than n≠t and incorrectly asserts A=n⊙_t B, whereas in general only n⊙_t B⊆A.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 3.4 and later uses such as Theorem 4.7
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper repeatedly assumes ultrafilters p in cl(E(K(βZ,+)))∩E(K(βZ,·)). On the semigroup (Z,·), 0 is a zero, so K(βZ,·)={0} and E(K(βZ,·))={0}; this principal ultrafilter is not in the additive minimal closure. Thus the assumed nonempty intersection does not exist on Z. The results would need to be formulated on N or Z*.

The theorem states every syndetic set in (Z,⊙_t) is additively piecewise syndetic. This is false: {t} is syndetic in (Z,⊙_t) because t is a zero, so t^{-1}{t}=Z, but {t} is not additively piecewise syndetic. The proof also allows s=t, making s−t=0 and the claimed equality A=s⊙_t C invalid.

The theorem claims every ⊙_t-piecewise syndetic set contains arithmetic progressions of arbitrary length. But {t} is thick in (Z,⊙_t), hence piecewise syndetic, because f⊙_t t=t for all f, and {t} contains no nontrivial arithmetic progression.

The proof says 'Now we choose any n∈Z\{t}' after stating {n:n^{-1}A∈q}∈p, but it must choose n from that p-large set. Moreover, after defining F'={1/(n-t)f:f∈F}, the proof uses a+(1/n)P(d) instead of a+(1/(n-t))P(d), and then applies n⊙_t(a+P(d)) rather than n⊙_t(a+(1/(n-t))P(d)).

With h(x)=x−t, the ring isomorphism is between (Z,+,·) and (Z,⊕_{-t},⊙_{-t}), so Theorem 3.4 should give \tilde h(p)∈cl(E(K(βZ,⊕_{-t})))∩E(K(βZ,⊙_{-t})), not ⊕_t,⊙_t. Also A−t∈\tilde h(p) should imply FS_{-t}∪σ_{-t}⊆A−t, not t+FS_{-t}∪t+σ_{-t}⊆A−t.

For l=1,k=-1, Definition 2.6 gives c⊙_{1,-1}d=cd−c−d+2, not cd+c+d. Therefore the advertised equations x+P(y−x)=z+w+zw and a+b=2(cd+c+d) are not the correct special cases for k=-1; they correspond to k=1.

The displayed system uses y_1⊕_{l,k}y_2⊕...⊕_{l,k}y_n, but the operation ⊕_{l,k} is never defined; only ⊕_t and ⊙_{l,k} are defined earlier. The proof is about central sets in (Z,⊙_{l,k}), so the finite products should use ⊙_{l,k}, not ⊕_{l,k}.
